she pronoun

also her

classical

Cic. Fam. 9.9.1: certum sciō jam convaluisse eam

is, ea, id

pronoun: feminine ea, eam, eā; genitive ejus, dative eī, declension

she, her (feminine ea)

As with “he”, the subject is mostly left out: Terentia minus bellē habuit, Terentia was a bit unwell, and then convaluisse eam, that she has recovered. Latin “she” follows grammatical gender, so a feminine noun is “she” in Latin where English says “it” (see it).

Other words

  • illa — she, that woman

    pronoun: feminine of ille · also used · classical · Phaedr. App. 32.5: salvē, inquit illa; Catull. 3.5: quem plūs illa oculīs suīs amābat

    For a woman spoken of with weight, or a new subject in a story: salvē, inquit illa.

  • haec — she, this woman (here)

    pronoun: feminine of hic · also used · classical

    The woman present or just named.

  • ista — she, that woman (near you)

    pronoun: feminine of iste · also used · classical

    See he.

Examples

  • Terentia minus bellē habuit, sed certum sciō jam convaluisse eam

    Terentia was a bit unwell, but I know for certain that she has now recovered.Cic. Fam. 9.9.1

  • salvē, inquit illa; cūr mē fūgistī, obsecrō?

    “Hello,” she said; “why did you run away from me, please?”Phaedr. App. 32.5

  • passer mortuus est meae puellae, passer, dēliciae meae puellae, quem plūs illa oculīs suīs amābat

    My girl’s sparrow is dead, the sparrow, my girl’s darling, which she loved more than her own eyes.Catull. 3.3–5

  • amābat enim sēcum praesentiam meam mōre mātrum

    For she loved to have me with her, as mothers do.Aug. Conf. 5.8.15

  • ōrō tē … mulier, sine eam tōtam integram mātrem esse fīliī suī

    I beg you, madam, let her be wholly and entirely the mother of her own son.Gell. 12.1.5

See also he, it, her, herself.
